executiveSummary: The reporting period highlights two high-urgency developments: quantified U.S. financial losses tied to AI-enabled scams, including voice-cloned distress and business email compromise (BEC), and uneven state-level protections against AI-generated political content heading into U.S. elections. These stress both consumer safety and institutional resilience across payment verification, identity assurance, and election integrity. View Article View Article Voice cloning remains a principal synthetic-media vector in fraud, with platform-level defenses emerging such as Android's call-authentication protections aimed at AI deepfake scam calls. Concurrent research signals increased realism and persuasion-particularly through emotionally expressive speech deepfakes-and warns that fully synthetic, text-to-video "fake news" could challenge newsroom verification workflows. View Article Supporting Report Supporting Report Regulatory momentum in the European Union has immediate operational implications: AI Act Article 50 deepfake transparency obligations now apply, requiring visible disclosures and machine-readable markings for synthetic content, though enforcement gaps may persist. Enterprises, platforms, and publishers should adapt provenance and disclosure workflows accordingly. View Article Supporting Report Overall, the environment appears to be worsening as quantified losses rise, political-communication risks escalate, and research advances both offensive realism and questions about watermark reliability. Near-term priorities include strengthened out-of-band verification, provenance adoption, and election-related content authentication. View Article
